identity.nameEn: Sri Bhramaramba Mallikarjuna Swamy Temple, Srisailam
identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Srisailam is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva, worshipped here as Mallikarjuna, and is simultaneously revered as a Shakti Peetha, where the goddess is worshipped as Bhramaramba Devi. The Andhra Pradesh government's own tourism description states that Srisailam is one of only two places in India — alongside Varanasi — where an ancient Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peetha coexist within a single temple, and notes that devotees are permitted to touch the lingam directly with hand or forehead, a practice not common to all twelve Jyotirlingas. Devotional and government-tourism accounts also connect the site to Adi Shankaracharya, who is traditionally said to have composed devotional verses near Srisailam. Sources vary on precisely which enumerated list of Shakti Peethas the shrine belongs to and its rank within it — the Government of India's national utsav.gov.in portal places it 6th among 18 Maha Shakti Peethas, while other reference material places it among the wider, differently-numbered list of Shakta pithas; this reflects genuinely competing classification traditions rather than a single settled count, and is recorded here as such.

governance.establishedEra: Satavahana-era inscriptions attest to the site from the 2nd century CE · Principal surviving temple fabric built under the Reddi kings (14th century CE) and substantially expanded under the Vijayanagara empire (14th–16th centuries CE)

narrative.summaryIntro:
The Sri Bhramaramba Mallikarjuna Swamy Temple stands on a hilltop in the Nallamala Hills at Srisailam, in Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh, overlooking the Krishna River. It is dedicated to Shiva, worshipped here as Mallikarjuna, and to his consort, worshipped as the goddess Bhramaramba — a rare pairing that makes the temple both one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and one of the Shakti Peethas of Hindu tradition.

Administered by the Sri Bhramaramba Mallikarjuna Swamy Varla Devasthanam under the Andhra Pradesh Endowments Department, the temple complex is enclosed by tall fortified walls with four gateway towers (gopurams) and preserves architectural and inscriptional evidence spanning the Satavahana, Reddi and Vijayanagara periods. In July 2026 the Archaeological Survey of India reported a newly identified Vijayanagara-era bas-relief on the temple's southern prakara wall depicting giraffes and camels, evidence that the site was also a medieval hub of long-distance trade alongside its role as a pilgrimage centre.
narrative.documentedHistory:
Inscriptional evidence of the Satavahana dynasty places a shrine at Srisailam as far back as the 2nd century CE. The temple's Wikipedia-sourced architectural account dates the core sanctum housing the Mallikarjuna lingam to the 7th century CE; this specific dating is not corroborated by any government source consulted here, and the Nandyal district administration's own tourism page instead states that construction of the temple occurred in the 14th century CE — the two accounts are not necessarily describing the same phase of building, but the discrepancy in dating is recorded here as unresolved.

The Reddi dynasty (c. 1325–1448 CE) is described as a golden age of patronage: Prolaya Vema Reddi is credited with major repairs to the temple and with building a flight of steps from the Krishna River up to the temple (Patala Ganga), and Anavema Reddi is credited with constructing the Veerasiromandapam, associated with Veerashaiva votive practice. Under the Vijayanagara empire, Harihara I (14th–15th centuries CE) undertook most of the temple's later structural additions, and Krishnadevaraya is credited with further mandapas and gopuram work.

In July 2026, the Archaeological Survey of India announced the identification of a rare bas-relief on the southern prakara (enclosure) wall of the temple depicting a procession of two giraffes and two camels with attendants, part of a set of narrative bas-reliefs the ASI dates to the 14th–16th centuries CE (the Vijayanagara period). The ASI states this and other finds, including copper plates and inscriptions reported from the Ghantamandapam area, indicate Srisailam functioned as a hub of medieval maritime trade with Africa and the Middle East in addition to its role as a pilgrimage centre.
associatedSaints: Adi Shankaracharya — traditionally said to have composed devotional verses near Srisailam (per Andhra Pradesh Tourism's description of the nearby Paladhara-Panchadhara site)

shrines.locationDescription: The main sanctum housing the self-manifest Mallikarjuna lingam. Dated to the 7th century CE per the temple's Wikipedia-sourced architectural account, but the Nandyal district government portal instead states the temple's construction occurred in the 14th century CE — the two accounts conflict and are recorded as such.
Shrine of the goddess Bhramaramba within the temple complex, the seat of the site's status as a Shakti Peetha alongside the Mallikarjuna sanctum's status as a Jyotirlinga.
A hall with intricately sculpted pillars, built during the Vijayanagara period.
A grouping of one thousand lingams within the complex, traditionally attributed to Rama; a further set of five lingams is traditionally attributed to the Pandavas.
A mandapa built under the Reddi king Anavema Reddi (Reddi dynasty, c. 1325–1448 CE), historically associated with Veerashaiva votive practice.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Bathing ghat on the Krishna River
shrines.locationDescription: A flight of steps down to the Krishna River, traditionally credited to the Reddi king Prolaya Vema Reddi; AP Tourism separately lists it as a sacred bathing spot roughly 1 km from the main temple.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Enclosure walls and four gateway towers
shrines.locationDescription: The temple's walled enclosure, reported as roughly 183 m by 152 m with walls about 8.5 m tall, spanning about two hectares with four gopurams. In July 2026 the Archaeological Survey of India identified a Vijayanagara-era (14th–16th century) bas-relief of two giraffes and two camels with attendants on a panel of the southern prakara wall, cited as evidence of the temple's medieval international trade links.

festivals.significance: The temple's principal annual festival, per the Government of India's utsav.gov.in event listing. Rituals described include Dhwajarohanam (flag-hoisting), a midnight Lingodbhava Maha Rudrabhishekam on the night of Maha Shivaratri itself, the Pagalankarana ceremony, Kalyanotsavam, multiple vahana (vehicle) processions, Rathotsavam (chariot procession) and Teppotsavam (float festival). The Government of India's Incredible India portal separately confirms Maha Shivaratri as the temple's key festival occasion.
